lines: {who} stood in the doorway, hat clutched in both hands.
"I know you've been asking about {event}. Please. Don't print it."
{who} knocked three times and waited a long while before coming in.
"I have family here. If it's printed, we can't go on living in this town."
{who} began to cry the moment {who.ta} came in, and could not get a whole sentence out.
In the end {who.ta} said only: "Don't write about me."
{who} sat down and rested both hands on {who.his} knees.
"I'll be plain with you. If {event} goes in the paper, nobody comes out ahead."
{who} spoke slowly, as if the words had been turned over all the way here.
"You want a paper that sells. I want a life I can still live. Can't we both give a little?"
{who} came in and slammed a hand down on the table, then looked sorry for it.
"I'm asking you. Just this once."
{who} did not sit, and spoke standing.
"I seldom ask anyone for anything. I am asking you to think this over."
{who} brought a bottle of good whiskey and set it on the type case.
"We are both respectable people in this town. Respectable people settle things respectably."
{who} said {who.ta} had prayed a long while over this last night.
"The Lord forgives. Why can't a newspaper?"
{who} first asked whether you had eaten.
Only then did {who.ta} say: "I know this is hard for you too. But could you leave {event} out of the paper?"
{who} looked you straight in the eye the whole time.
"If you do me this one favor, I'll remember it. If you don't, I'll remember that too."
{who} set a parcel down by the door. It was bread, baked at home.
"I didn't come to beg. All right. I did."
{who} stood at the door a while before coming in.
"I know what you've been asking about. I ask only one thing: leave my name out of it."
{who} came in without any small talk.
"Please."
{who} did not come in. "Print certain things, and the windows of this office get hard to keep in one piece."
{who} stood in the doorway and spoke quietly.
"A word of advice. There are things you would do better to forget, once you know them."
{who} shoved the door so hard it banged against the wall.
"Keep digging, and I'll show you how deep the Grey River is."
{who} lit a cigarette in the doorway and finished it before saying a word.
"This place is built of wood, isn't it?"
{who} said nothing at all, set a brick on your desk, and left.
{who} stood outside the office and cursed for a quarter of an hour while the neighbors came out to watch.
At last {who.ta} said: "You just wait."
{who} sat down and spoke calmly.
"Your paper lives on advertising. Have you ever thought about who buys the advertisements?"
{who} kept glancing at the license on your wall while {who.ta} spoke.
"That license was issued by the town hall. What the town hall gives, it can take back."
{who} did not sit.
"I know the judges at the state capital. Whom do you know?"
{who} sent a man instead of coming in person.
The man said: "I was asked to pass along a word. Know when to stop."
{who} came in smiling and sat down smiling.
"Running a paper all on your own can't be easy. Watch your step walking home at night."
{who} made it very plain.
"Print it, and I'll see to it you never print anything again. That's not a threat. It's a fact."
{who} set down an envelope with {offer} dollars in it.
"Leave me out of it this week. And next week."
{who} said: "I know you're short of money. Take {offer} dollars, and this is the end of it."
{who} came to talk business: {offer} dollars in exchange for keeping {event} out of the paper.
{who} came straight to the point: "Here are {offer} dollars. That buys one issue without my name in it."
{who} offered to take out half a year of advertising, with {offer} dollars paid in advance.
"There's only one condition, and you know what it is."
{who} brought no money, only a sheet of paper.
"This is a printing job for next year, worth {offer} dollars. Sign it, and we'll forget the other matter."
{who} tucked {offer} dollars under an old book.
"The book is a gift. Whatever's inside it, you can look at for yourself."
{who} put the money on the table and made for the door, then turned back.
"It's {offer} dollars. Is it enough? If it isn't, I'll find more."
{who} counted out the money while talking.
"That makes {offer} dollars. Everyone has a price, and yours I can pay."
{who} said: "I'm not buying you. Call the {offer} dollars help with your roof."
{who} came by to say thank you, and on the way out said quietly: "{fact}."
{who} brought a basket of eggs.
Setting it down, {who.ta} said: "One more thing you might want to know. {fact}."
{who} sat down and would not leave, talking of the weather and then of the market.
At last {who.ta} leaned in: "{fact}. I'm telling nobody but you."
{who} said one sentence and left: "{fact}."
{who} said: "You were fair to me last time. I'll be fair to you. {fact}."
{who} pressed a folded note into your hand at the door. It read: "{fact}."
{who.ta} left without coming in.
{who} came by to say thank you, with a basket of eggs.
{who} sat in the office a while and said the last report was well done.
On the way out, {who.ta} said: "If you ever need anything, come and find me."
{who} brought a jar of home-pickled vegetables by way of thanks.
{who} said {who.ta} would pray for the paper at church.
{who} called to explain for half an hour, and said what was printed was not the whole story.
{who} said: "I know you wrote what you saw. I only want you to see the other side."
{who} sat in the office all afternoon and finally said: "That's all I have to say. Print it or don't."
{who} brought a stack of receipts and laid them out on the desk one by one.
"Look, this is how it was." {who.ta} talked until dark.
{who} spoke so softly you had to lean close to hear.
"I'm not that kind of person. Truly I'm not."
{who} said: "I won't take action over what you printed. But you ought to know the whole picture."
Then {who.ta} told a story quite different from the one in the paper.
{who} arrived shouting.
When the shouting was over, {who.ta} sat down and said a few honest things.
{who} did not blame you.
"What you wrote is true. I only wanted to tell you why."
{who} said {who.ta} had already been to church to confess.
"I did wrong. But I'm not a wicked person."
{who} gave an explanation that sounded perfectly reasonable.
Only when you saw {who.him} to the door did you notice that {who.ta} had not denied a single thing.
{who} spoke through gritted teeth: "If you're going to print it, print all of it. {fact}."
{who} said: "You printed me. Don't let the others off. {fact}."
{who} slapped a sheet of paper down on the desk: "{fact}. Have you got the nerve to print that?"
{who} was very calm.
"If everyone's to be shamed, let's all be shamed together. {fact}."
{who} kept a fist clenched the whole time {who.ta} talked.
"Why only me? {fact}. Go and look into that!"
{who} smiled: "Let me give you a bigger one. {fact}."
{who} came wanting to tell tales on someone else, but had nothing to tell.
{who} sat for ages and cursed several people, but said nothing you didn't already know.
"And another thing. {fact}."
"There's more. {fact}."
{who.ta} added: "{fact}."
{who} wants to place an advertisement in the next issue.
{who} says the earlier trouble is over, and the advertisement can run as before.
{who} came to renew the advertisement, in the same spot as always.
{who} says a new shipment of cloth has come in, and wants to advertise it.
{who} says the tavern is having a fiddler in on Saturday, and wants to post a notice.
{who} says the sawmill is taking on hands, and wants to run a notice in the paper.
{who} came, stood in the doorway a while, and left without a word.
A knock at the door. You opened it, and there was {who}. {who.ta} looked at you once and turned away.
{who} came in and sat on the bench for a quarter of an hour without saying anything. On leaving, {who.ta} closed the door gently.
{who} left an old copy of the paper on the step: the issue that printed the story about {subject.short}. It had been badly crumpled.
Someone was standing outside the window. It was {who}. By the time you went out, {who.ta} was far down the street.
{who} came after dark and drew the curtains before saying anything.
"{subject.short} has been saying at the tavern there's a score to settle with you. Be careful."
{who} said: "I shouldn't have come. But you ought to know {subject.short} has been asking what time you go to bed."
{who} did not sit down: "Stay away from the back alley. There are people working for {subject.short} hanging about there."
{who} said a single sentence and went: "Bolt your door these next few nights."
{who} said {subject.short} has looked very black these last days. "I don't know what {subject.ta} means to do. I'm only telling you."
{who} stood at the door a long time before speaking. "I came on {subject.short}'s account. {subject.he} doesn't know I'm here."
"Please don't print {event}. If {subject.he} loses the work, how is the family to manage?"
{who} brought a basket of eggs, set it down and would not take it back.
"{subject.short} did wrong. But {subject.he} is family. Leave {subject.him} a way to go on."
{who} spoke very quietly, as if afraid the neighbours would hear.
"{subject.short} hasn't eaten in two days. Could you at least keep the name out of it?"
{who} cried first, and only afterwards said it was about {subject.short}.
"There are children in the house. If it's in the paper, how do they hold their heads up at school?"
{who} said {who.he} had prayed a long while in church on Sunday for {subject.short}.
"If you can leave {event} out of the paper, the Lord will remember it. So will I."
{who} sat down and said it plainly first: "I'm not here to defend {subject.short}."
"I only ask you to think how the rest of the family is to live in this town once it's printed."
{who} came in red in the face, as if {who.he} had argued with {who.him}self all the way.
"Must you print {subject.short}'s business? ... I'm asking you. Don't."
